Is there a Claude/Code CLI slash command to see a diff of changed files, and why doesn't /diff show the diff content?

Short answer: /diff exists; the "New file not yet staged" message for untracked files is a side effect of the Current tab being git diff HEAD under the hood, not intentional concealment — git has no index entry to diff an untracked file against.
Is there a Claude/Code CLI slash command to see a diff of changed files, and why doesn't /diff show the diff content?

Per the official reference, /diff has two kinds of tabs: Current (git diff HEAD, all uncommitted changes) and per-turn (T1, T2, …, individual Claude turns). The docs describe switching between them but don't specify the per-turn tabs' data source.
Is there a Claude/Code CLI slash command to see a diff of changed files, and why doesn't /diff show the diff content?

Unconfirmed in official docs (seen on a third-party blog): per-turn tabs may reconstruct edits from the conversation record rather than from git, which would let them show new-file content without staging first. Worth testing empirically — arrow to a turn tab (e.g. T6) for an untracked file instead of Current.

Is there any equivalent functionality in Claude/Code's CLI to Claude/Desktop/Code's ability to group related chat histories together?
Answer/Official from Manage Claude Code sessions and Agent view:
Is there any equivalent functionality in Claude/Code's CLI to Claude/Desktop/Code's ability to group related chat histories together?

Short answer: Nothing in the CLI matches Desktop's Code-tab sidebar (explicit repo/branch/worktree badges) directly, but the CLI has two mechanisms that get most of the way there: automatic directory-scoped grouping of session history, and an agent view (claude agents) that groups sessions by state or by directory.
Is there any equivalent functionality in Claude/Code's CLI to Claude/Desktop/Code's ability to group related chat histories together?

Directory-scoped grouping (implicit): the CLI stores each session transcript under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl, keyed by working-directory path. Every session run from a given repo therefore already sits together on disk — an implicit grouping by project rather than an explicit tag or folder.
Is there any equivalent functionality in Claude/Code's CLI to Claude/Desktop/Code's ability to group related chat histories together?

Session picker: /resume (or claude --resume) opens a picker scoped to the current directory by default. From there: Ctrl+W expands to all worktrees, Ctrl+A expands to all projects on the machine, Ctrl+B filters by git branch, and text search matches names/summaries/PR URLs. Sessions can also be given a name (claude -n <name> or /rename) so related ones are easier to pick out.
Is there any equivalent functionality in Claude/Code's CLI to Claude/Desktop/Code's ability to group related chat histories together?

Agent view (closest analogue): claude agents opens a richer view that groups sessions either by state (Pinned, Ready for review, Needs input, Working, Completed — toggle with Ctrl+S) or by directory. Sessions can be pinned (Ctrl+T) to keep related ones at the top, filtered by agent name/state/PR number, and reordered within a group.
Is there any equivalent functionality in Claude/Code's CLI to Claude/Desktop/Code's ability to group related chat histories together?

What's still missing: no free-form tagging, no cross-repo logical grouping (grouping stays either state-based or directory-based, never topic-based), and no visual per-session metadata badges (repo/branch/worktree/env) like Desktop's Code tab shows in its sidebar.

What can the Microsoft 365 connector for Claude/Code do when viewing Excel sheets?

Short answer: There is no Excel-specific, cell-addressed tool. The Microsoft 365 connector treats an Excel workbook as an ordinary file in OneDrive/SharePoint: Claude Code finds it via search and opens and reads its content (sheet data, tables, text) via read_resource. It can analyze what it reads. It cannot edit individual cells or formulas in place — writes are whole-file operations, and only when the optional write tools are enabled. Everything is scoped to your own Microsoft 365 permissions.

What does the skill listing truncation warning in Claude/Code mean?
What does the skill listing truncation warning in Claude/Code mean?

What the message is: At the start of a turn, Claude Code injects a skill listing into the model context: each discoverable skill’s name plus (normally) its description and when_to_use text so the model knows what exists and when to load it. When that listing would use more than your configured share of the context window, the CLI drops full descriptions for the least-recently-used skills and keeps full text only for skills it considers most-used, then prints the warning you saw (with counts and an estimate of how much of the window the full listing would have taken versus the cap).
What does the skill listing truncation warning in Claude/Code mean?

Where it comes from: This behavior is implemented in Claude Code itself (not your shell). It is controlled by settings documented on Claude Code settings: skillListingBudgetFraction reserves a fraction of the model’s context window for that listing (default 0.01 = 1%). When the listing would exceed the budget, descriptions for the least-used skills are collapsed to bare names so the model can still invoke them but no longer sees why. A companion cap, maxSkillDescriptionChars (default 1536), truncates each skill’s combined description + when_to_use text before the overall budget is applied. See the same settings table rows and the skills guide Extend Claude with skills (frontmatter reference explains the listing and per-skill truncation).
What does the skill listing truncation warning in Claude/Code mean?

How to read the parenthetical (example 3.2% / 1%): The first figure is an estimate of how much of the context the full skill metadata would consume; the second is your current budget (often the default 1%). The gap is why many descriptions were dropped in one shot.
What does the skill listing truncation warning in Claude/Code mean?

What you can do: Raise skillListingBudgetFraction in ~/.claude/settings.json (or project or local settings) to keep more descriptions at the cost of more tokens every turn and faster consumption of rate limits—the message’s “~6k tokens” line is that tradeoff spelled out. Alternatively reduce load: shorten description / when_to_use in SKILL.md files, disable plugins or skills you do not need (the message points at /skills and the skillOverrides mechanism described in the skills doc), or raise maxSkillDescriptionChars only if individual skills are being cut short. For visibility into what was truncated, the settings doc says /doctor shows the current truncation count and which skills are affected.

What is the difference between the schedule command in Claude Code CLI and Claude/Routines in Claude/Desktop/Code?
What is the difference between the schedule command in Claude Code CLI and Claude/Routines in Claude/Desktop/Code?
Answer/Official from Automate work with routines and Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Code Desktop:
What is the difference between the schedule command in Claude Code CLI and Claude/Routines in Claude/Desktop/Code?

Short answer: Desktop's Routines page is the umbrella UI for two different scheduling mechanisms under one name — Cloud routines and Local scheduled tasks. The CLI's /schedule command only reaches one of those two — Cloud routines — and has no facility at all for the other.
What is the difference between the schedule command in Claude Code CLI and Claude/Routines in Claude/Desktop/Code?

Cloud routines — the part they share: Desktop → Routines → New routine → Cloud, and CLI /schedule, both write to the same account-level list at claude.ai/code/routines. Either surface can create, list, edit, or run these; they are literally the same saved routines, just two front ends onto one backend. Runs happen unattended on Anthropic's cloud infrastructure — no permission-mode picker, no approval prompts — scoped instead by the routine's selected repositories, cloud environment, and connectors.
What is the difference between the schedule command in Claude Code CLI and Claude/Routines in Claude/Desktop/Code?

Local scheduled tasks — the part /schedule cannot touch: Desktop → Routines → New routine → Local creates a task that runs on the user's own machine, persisted as ~/.claude/scheduled-tasks/<task-name>/SKILL.md. These have a permission-mode/model picker and use local MCP connectors and local files — the opposite of a cloud routine's autonomy. The CLI has no command, flag, or tool that lists, creates, edits, or deletes these; CronList in a CLI session only reports a third, unrelated mechanism (session-local jobs from /loop/CronCreate, which expire after 7 days and disappear when the conversation ends).
What is the difference between the schedule command in Claude Code CLI and Claude/Routines in Claude/Desktop/Code?

Even within Cloud routines, /schedule is narrower than the web UI: the CLI command only configures the schedule trigger. Adding API or GitHub-event triggers to a cloud routine requires the web editor at claude.ai/code/routines.
What is the difference between the schedule command in Claude Code CLI and Claude/Routines in Claude/Desktop/Code?

See Claude/Routine for the full mechanism (what's saved, trigger types, run lifecycle, limits) and its Misconceptions section, which calls out this exact confusion directly: "Routines are the same as /loop or local Desktop schedules" is false — /loop and Desktop Local tasks both run on the local machine, while Routines (whether created from Desktop's Cloud option or from CLI /schedule) are remote cloud sessions.

Why does piping claude --help to bat break keyboard scrolling while mise --help works fine?
Why does piping claude --help to bat break keyboard scrolling while mise --help works fine?

Short answer: yes, this is a Claude/Code-specific bug, not a bat misconfiguration. Claude/Code enables an enhanced keyboard-input protocol (the kitty keyboard protocol / xterm's modifyOtherKeys, aka XTMODKEYS) on the terminal and doesn't always restore it afterward. The piped --help text itself carries no escape bytes — the terminal is left in this altered input mode from Claude Code's own terminal setup, so it mangles what less (bat's underlying pager) reads back from the keyboard.
